items.en: The Ten Perceptions: Sequence of Stages, and Impermanence, Suffering, No-Self
items.zh: 十想 · 次位 · 無常想苦想無我想

zh: 次釋十想法門。十想者：一、無常想；二、苦想；三、無我想；四、食不淨想；五、一切世間不可樂想；六、死想；七、不淨想；八、斷想；九、離想；十、盡想。今釋十想，即為三意：一、明次位；二、明修證；三、明趣道想。
en: Next, explaining the dharma-gate of the ten perceptions. The ten perceptions are: first, the perception of impermanence; second, the perception of suffering; third, the perception of no-self; fourth, the perception of the impurity of food; fifth, the perception that nothing in the whole world is to be delighted in; sixth, the perception of death; seventh, the perception of impurity; eighth, the perception of cessation; ninth, the perception of detachment; tenth, the perception of exhaustion. Explaining the ten perceptions now has three senses: first, clarifying their sequence of stages; second, clarifying their cultivation and realization; third, clarifying how they lead toward the path.

zh: 第一、所言次位者，於佛教所說諸法中有三種道：一、見道；二、修道；三、無學道。今此十想即約三道以明位次。所以者何？壞法人於乾慧地已具九想，伏諸結使，今修無常等三想，即是總相觀，為破六十二見諸顛倒法，入見道中，得初果故。次有食不淨想等四想，此為須陀洹、斯陀含人入修道中欲斷五下分結，證阿那含果故，說是四種別相事觀，助成正觀，斷思惟惑。後斷、離、盡等三想，為阿那含人行阿羅漢向，修無學道，為欲斷離色、無色愛，證阿羅漢故說。當知十想約三道以辯次位，一往義則可見。
en: First, as for their sequence of stages: among the dharmas explained within the Buddha's teaching, there are three kinds of path — first, the path of seeing; second, the path of cultivation; third, the path of no-more-learning. These ten perceptions here are clarified in their sequence of stages precisely with reference to these three paths.

Why is this? The practitioner of the destructive path, already at the stage of dry wisdom, has already become complete with the nine contemplations and subdued the fetters; now, cultivating the first three perceptions — impermanence and the rest — this is precisely the general-mark contemplation, breaking through the sixty-two views and every inverted dharma, and entering the path of seeing, thereby obtaining the first fruit. Next come the four perceptions beginning with the impurity of food; these are for the stream-enterer and the once-returner, entering the path of cultivation, wishing to sever the five lower fetters and realize the fruit of non-returning — hence these four kinds of particular-mark contemplation of concrete matters are explained, assisting the correct contemplation to come to completion and severing the afflictions of thought. Last come the three perceptions of cessation, detachment, and exhaustion; these are for the non-returner, proceeding toward arhatship, cultivating the path of no-more-learning, wishing to sever and depart from craving for the form and formless realms, and realize arhatship — hence these are explained here. One should know, then, that the ten perceptions are distinguished in their sequence of stages with reference to these three paths; in a general sense, this may be seen for itself.

zh: 第二、明修證。一、無常想者，觀一切有為法無常，智慧相應故，名無常想。所以者何？一切有為法新新生滅故，屬因緣故，不增積故，生時無所從來，滅時無所去處，故名無常。是中無常有二種：一者、眾生無常；二者、世界無常。眾生無常者，行者觀我及一切眾生從歌羅邏來，色心生滅變異，乃至老死無暫停時。所以者何？一切有為悉屬生、住、滅三相遷變，故知無常。所謂欲生異生，欲住異住，欲滅異滅，如是變易無常，剎那迅速，無暫停息，故知一切眾生悉皆無常。世界無常者，如偈說：
en: Second, clarifying cultivation and realization. First, the perception of impermanence: contemplating that every conditioned dharma is impermanent, wisdom corresponding to this very contemplation — hence it is named the perception of impermanence. Why is this? Every conditioned dharma arises and ceases ever anew, belongs to causes and conditions, and does not accumulate or increase; at the moment of its arising, it comes from nowhere at all, and at the moment of its ceasing, it goes nowhere at all — hence it is named impermanence.

Within this, impermanence is of two kinds: first, the impermanence of sentient beings; second, the impermanence of the world. As for the impermanence of sentient beings: the practitioner contemplates that both oneself and every sentient being, ever since the kalala-stage, undergo form and mind arising, ceasing, and transforming, all the way through old age and death, without a single moment's pause. Why is this? Every conditioned thing belongs, entirely, to the three marks of arising, abiding, and ceasing, shifting and changing — hence one knows it to be impermanent. That is: wishing to arise, it instead arises as something already different; wishing to abide, it instead abides as something already different; wishing to cease, it instead ceases as something already different — change and impermanence of this kind, swift as an instant, without a single moment's rest — hence one knows that every sentient being, without exception, is impermanent. As for the impermanence of the world, the verse says:

zh:
大地草木皆磨滅，須彌巨海亦崩竭，
諸天住處皆燒盡，爾時世界何處常？
復次，如佛說無常觀有二種：一者、有餘；二者、無餘。一切人物皆盡，唯有名在，是名有餘；若人物滅盡，是名無餘。所以者何？若言以三相故，一切有為法為無常者，三相自不可得，云何有無常？如生時無住滅，離生時亦無住滅。若生時即有住滅，即壞生相，以生滅相違故。若言離生有滅住，亦壞三相義。若離生則滅，無所滅故。當知三相不可得。若無有三相，云何言無常？若不得無常相，即見聖道，是名無常想。
en:
"The great earth, the grasses and trees, all alike are ground away; Mount Sumeru and the great ocean, too, collapse and run dry;
every heavenly dwelling-place is burned entirely away — at such a time, where, then, does the world remain constant?"

Furthermore, as the Buddha teaches, the contemplation of impermanence is of two kinds: first, impermanence with remainder; second, impermanence without remainder. Every person and thing entirely exhausted, only the name remaining — this is named with remainder; should person and thing alike be utterly extinguished — this is named without remainder.

Why is this? Should one say that, on account of the three marks, every conditioned dharma is impermanent, then the three marks themselves cannot be found at all — how, then, could there be impermanence? For, at the moment of arising, there is no abiding or ceasing; and apart from the moment of arising, too, there is no abiding or ceasing. Should arising itself already possess abiding and ceasing, this would destroy the very mark of arising, since arising and ceasing contradict one another. Should one say that, apart from arising, there is ceasing and abiding, this, too, destroys the sense of the three marks. Should there be ceasing apart from arising, there would be nothing there to cease at all. One should know, then, that the three marks cannot be found. If there are no three marks at all, how, then, can one speak of impermanence? Should one fail to find any mark of impermanence at all, this is precisely seeing the noble path — this is named the perception of impermanence.

zh: 問曰：若爾，佛何故說無常為聖諦？答曰：為對治破著常顛倒故，是中不應求實，若心計無常為實者，即墮斷見。復次，有餘無常想，如上特勝、通明中說；無餘者，在下慧行中當廣說。問曰：何以聖行初門先說無常想？答曰：一切凡夫未見道時，各貴所行，或言持戒為重，或言多聞為重，或言十二頭陀為重，或言禪定為重。如是各各所行為貴，更不復勤求涅槃。佛言：「是諸功德皆是趣涅槃道分，若觀諸法無常，是為真涅槃道。」如是種種因緣故，諸法雖空，而說是無常想。
en: Question: if this is so, why does the Buddha teach impermanence as a noble truth? Answer: this is in order to counteract and break through the inverted view of clinging to permanence — within this, one ought not to seek any reality at all; should the mind reckon impermanence itself to be real, one thereby falls into the view of annihilation. Furthermore, the perception of impermanence with remainder is as already explained above, within the special excellences and the thorough-and-bright contemplation; impermanence without remainder will be explained at greater length below, within the section on wisdom-practice.

Question: why does the very first gate of noble practice speak of the perception of impermanence first? Answer: every ordinary person, before seeing the path, prizes their own particular practice above the rest — some say upholding the precepts is what matters most, some say extensive learning is what matters most, some say the twelve austere practices are what matter most, some say dhyāna concentration is what matters most. Each, prizing their own particular practice in this way, no longer diligently seeks nirvāṇa itself. The Buddha says: "All of these merits alike are but a portion of the path leading toward nirvāṇa; contemplating that every dharma is impermanent — this alone is the true path to nirvāṇa." For causes and conditions of this kind, though every dharma is empty, the perception of impermanence is nonetheless taught.

zh: 二、苦想者，行者應作是思惟：若一切有餘法無常遷變，即是苦想。所以者何？從內六情、外六塵和合故，生六種識。六種識中生三種受，謂苦受、樂受、捨受。是三種受中生、老、病、死、恩愛別離、求不得、怨憎會、五陰盛等八苦之所逼切，故名為苦。復次，是苦受以事即是苦故，一切眾生所不欲；是樂受以為順情故，一切眾生所愛。若生貪著，無常敗壞，即現受眾苦，後受地獄、畜生、餓鬼等苦。如是等種種諸苦，皆從求樂生，故知樂即是苦。捨受雖復情中不覺苦樂，不取不棄，理實無常遷逼，亦為大苦。如是觀時，於三界中不見樂相可生貪著，心生厭畏，是名苦想。問曰：若無常即是苦者，道聖諦有為無常亦應是苦。答曰：道聖諦雖無常，而能滅苦，不生諸著，又與空、無我等諸智慧和合故，但是無常，而非苦也。
en: Second, the perception of suffering: the practitioner should reflect thus: that every dharma with remainder, in its own impermanent shifting and changing, is itself precisely the perception of suffering. Why is this? From the union of the internal six faculties and the external six sense-objects, the six kinds of consciousness arise; within these six kinds of consciousness, three kinds of sensation arise, namely painful sensation, pleasant sensation, and neutral sensation. Within these three kinds of sensation, one is pressed and afflicted by the eight sufferings — birth, old age, illness, death, separation from what one loves, failing to obtain what one seeks, union with what one hates, and the flourishing of the five aggregates of clinging themselves — hence this is named suffering.

Furthermore, painful sensation, being in itself a matter of suffering, is something no sentient being desires; pleasant sensation, being agreeable to one's own feeling, is something every sentient being loves. Should craving and attachment arise toward it, its impermanent ruin thereupon brings the immediate experience of manifold sufferings, and, afterward, the suffering of hell, of the animal realm, and of the hungry ghosts as well. Every kind of suffering such as this arises entirely from the very seeking of pleasure — hence one knows that pleasure is itself suffering. Neutral sensation, though it is, within one's own feeling, aware of neither pain nor pleasure, neither grasped nor cast away, is nonetheless, in truth and in principle, impermanent and ever shifting and pressing upon one — this, too, is a great suffering.

Contemplating in this way, one sees, throughout the three realms, no mark of pleasure whatsoever capable of giving rise to craving and attachment, and the mind thereby gives rise to weariness and aversion — this is named the perception of suffering. Question: if impermanence is itself suffering, then the noble truth of the path, too, being conditioned and impermanent, ought likewise to be suffering. Answer: though the noble truth of the path is impermanent, it is nonetheless able to extinguish suffering, giving rise to no attachment whatsoever, and, moreover, is joined together with the wisdom of emptiness, no-self, and the rest — hence it is merely impermanent, and not suffering.

zh: 三、無我想者，行者當深思惟：若有為法悉是苦者，苦即是無我。所以者何？五受陰中悉皆是苦。若是苦者，即不自在；若不自在，是則無我。何以故？若有我自在者，則不應為苦所逼，知苦即是無我。復次，五陰、十二入、十八界中，諸法從緣生，則無自性故。若即陰離陰，更求我等十六知見，皆不可得。既不得我，則捨一切諸見執著，心無所取，便得解脫，是名無我想。是無常、苦、無我三想，觀行深細，在下釋苦諦中更當廣說。
en: Third, the perception of no-self: the practitioner should deeply reflect thus: should every conditioned dharma be, entirely, suffering, then suffering is itself precisely no-self. Why is this? Within the five aggregates of clinging, all alike are suffering; being suffering, one is thereby without freedom of one's own; being without freedom of one's own, this is precisely no-self. Why is this? Should there be a self possessing freedom of its own, it ought not to be pressed and afflicted by suffering at all — hence one knows that suffering is itself precisely no-self.

Furthermore, within the five aggregates, the twelve sense-bases, and the eighteen elements, every dharma arises from conditions, and thus possesses no nature of its own. Whether identical to the aggregates or separate from the aggregates, seeking further for a self through the sixteen forms of knowledge and view, none whatsoever can be found. A self being nowhere found, one thereupon relinquishes every view and every attachment, the mind grasping at nothing at all, and thereby obtains liberation — this is named the perception of no-self. These three perceptions of impermanence, suffering, and no-self involve a contemplative practice both deep and subtle, and will be explained at still greater length below, within the explanation of the truth of suffering.

zh: 問曰：無常、苦、無我，為是一事，為是三事？若是一事，一事不應說三；若是三事，佛何故說無常即苦，苦即無我？答：三是一事，所謂受有漏法。觀門分別故，有三種異：無常行相應，是無常想；苦行相應，是苦想；無我行相應，是無我想。無常不令入三界，苦令知三界過罪，無我則捨世間。復次，無常生厭，苦生怖畏，無我拔出，令得解脫。復次，無常者遮常見，苦遮令世涅槃見，無我者遮著處見。無常者，世間所可著常法是；苦者，世間計樂處是；無我者，世間所可計我牢固者是。如是等種種分別，並如《摩訶衍》中廣說也。
en: Question: are impermanence, suffering, and no-self a single matter, or are they three separate matters? Should they be a single matter, a single matter ought not to be spoken of as three; should they be three separate matters, why does the Buddha teach that impermanence is itself suffering, and suffering is itself no-self? Answer: the three are a single matter, namely the experiencing of a contaminated dharma. Through the distinctions made by the gate of contemplation, there come to be three differences: correspondence with the practice of impermanence is the perception of impermanence; correspondence with the practice of suffering is the perception of suffering; correspondence with the practice of no-self is the perception of no-self. Impermanence keeps one from entering the three realms; suffering causes one to know the fault belonging to the three realms; no-self, then, causes one to relinquish the world entirely.

Furthermore, impermanence gives rise to weariness; suffering gives rise to fear; no-self draws one out, causing one to obtain liberation. Furthermore, impermanence blocks the view of permanence; suffering blocks the view that takes the world itself for nirvāṇa; no-self blocks the view of attachment to any fixed place at all. Impermanence is precisely that permanent dharma which the world clings to; suffering is precisely that place of pleasure which the world reckons upon; no-self is precisely that solid, fixed self which the world reckons upon. Distinctions of every such kind are all explained at greater length in the Mahāyāna treatise.

The chain-argument linking impermanence, suffering, and no-self — impermanent, therefore suffering; impermanent and suffering, therefore not under one's own control, therefore not a self — is one of the oldest formal arguments in Buddhist philosophy, and this treatise's own treatment of it is notably austere: it explicitly rejects taking impermanence itself as a metaphysically "real" ground (reckoning impermanence itself as real, the text warns, falls into the view of annihilation), insisting instead that finding no fixed mark of impermanence at all is what actually counts as seeing the path. The staged-question format — question, then answer, repeatedly — is doing real philosophical work here rather than serving as mere rhetorical decoration, anticipating the two most natural objections a careful reader would raise (why call the noble path itself, which is also conditioned, "impermanent" but not "suffering"; and whether these three are really one thing or three) before they're asked.

quiz.q: What are the ten perceptions, in order?
options: impermanence, suffering, no-self, impurity of food, no delight in the world, death, impurity, cessation, detachment, exhaustion
quiz.why: The ten are impermanence, suffering, no-self, impurity of food, no delight in the world, death, impurity, cessation, detachment, and exhaustion.

quiz.q: By which three paths are the stages explained, and why are the first three cultivated?
options: seeing, cultivation, no-more-learning; the first three are general-mark contemplation breaking the sixty-two views to enter seeing and the first fruit
quiz.why: Using the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning; the first three are a general-mark contemplation that breaks the sixty-two views, entering seeing and the first fruit.

quiz.q: For whom are the four perceptions beginning with impurity of food taught, and why?
options: stream-enterers and once-returners in cultivation, to sever the five lower fetters; particular-mark contemplations aiding the correct one
ordinary people to see the path
quiz.why: They are for stream-enterers and once-returners in the path of cultivation, to sever the five lower fetters and attain non-returning, aiding the correct contemplation. C is the last three.

quiz.q: What are the two kinds of impermanence, and how is the world's impermanence described?
options: of beings and of the world; the earth ground away, Sumeru and the sea collapsing, the heavens burned
quiz.why: Impermanence is of beings and of the world; the verse says the earth is ground away, Sumeru and the ocean collapse, the heavens burn—where is the world constant?

quiz.q: How are impermanence "with remainder" and "without remainder" distinguished?
options: people and things gone but the name remains is with remainder; all utterly extinguished is without
quiz.why: When people and things are gone but their names remain, that is with remainder; when they are utterly extinguished, without remainder.

quiz.q: Having shown the three marks unfindable, what does the text conclude?
options: without the three marks how speak of impermanence; not finding its mark is seeing the noble path
quiz.why: The three marks cannot be found; without them how can one speak of impermanence? Not finding the mark of impermanence is seeing the noble path.

quiz.q: If impermanence is unfindable, why does the Buddha teach it as a noble truth?
options: to counteract clinging to permanence; one should not take it as real, or one falls into annihilationism
quiz.why: It is taught to counteract the inverted clinging to permanence; one should not seek reality in it, for taking impermanence as real is annihilationism.

quiz.q: Why does the noble practice begin with the perception of impermanence?
options: ordinary people prize their own practices and neglect nirvāṇa; the Buddha says contemplating impermanence is the true path
quiz.why: Each prizes precepts, learning, austerities, or dhyāna and stops seeking nirvāṇa; the Buddha says these are only parts of the path, and contemplating impermanence is the true path.

quiz.q: How does the text show that pleasure is suffering and neutral sensation too?
options: all suffering comes from seeking pleasure; neutral sensation, though unfelt, is impermanent and pressing
quiz.why: All kinds of suffering arise from seeking pleasure, so pleasure is suffering; neutral sensation, though felt as neither, is in principle impermanent and pressing, also great suffering.

quiz.q: The truth of the path is conditioned and impermanent; why is it not suffering?
options: it extinguishes suffering, gives rise to no attachment, and is joined with the wisdom of emptiness and no-self
quiz.why: Though impermanent, the path extinguishes suffering, produces no attachment, and is joined with the wisdom of emptiness and no-self, so it is impermanent but not suffering.

quiz.q: How does the perception of no-self reason?
options: the aggregates are suffering; suffering is unfree; unfree is no-self; a free self would not be oppressed
quiz.why: The aggregates are suffering; what is suffering is not free; what is not free is no-self; a self with freedom would not be pressed by suffering.

quiz.q: Are impermanence, suffering, and no-self one matter or three?
options: one matter, the experiencing of contaminated dharmas, differentiated by gates of contemplation
quiz.why: The three are one matter, the experiencing of contaminated dharmas; as gates of contemplation they differ according to which aspect one corresponds with.

quiz.q: What does each of the three give rise to?
options: impermanence weariness, suffering fear, no-self drawing out to liberation
quiz.why: Impermanence gives rise to weariness, suffering to fear, and no-self draws one out to liberation.
